newsitem.title: USA: Construction spending down broadly in December.
newsitem.headline: Construction spending down broadly in December.

text.p: Spending on new construction dropped in December for the first time in five months, the Commerce Department said Monday, as both government and privately financed building projects slowed.

Total spending on construction dropped 0.7 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $587.7 billion after a revised jump of 2 percent in November that previously was reported as a 1.9 percent increase.
It was the first decline in monthly construction spending since July, when it eased by 0.7 percent.

The falloff in December spending was widespread, down 0.5 percent to a rate of $441.5 billion for privately financed projects after a 2.2 percent November increase and down 1.3 percent to $146.1 billion for government spending after a 1.3 percent rise in November.
Bitter weather in much of the country during December may have played a role in the monthly decline.
For the full year 1996, construction spending was up 3.9 percent to $568.68 billion, compared with increases of 4.1 percent in each of 1994 and 1995.

During December, spending on new housing was up to an annual rate of $248 billion from $247 billion in November. But spending to put up new non-residential construction fell to $151.2 billion from $154.1 billion.
Government spending on construction projects dropped for sewer systems and water treatment plants as well as for housing and redevelopment.
After allowing for inflation, total construction spending was down 1 percent in December to a seasonally adjusted $505.9 billion annual rate after a 1.8 percent rise in November, the department said.
